plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: It is strict about what must be delivered and open about how. Genre, camera and scope were mine to decide, while the hard requirements (a 10-foot controller-first UX, the attract mode's 10-second rule, a dev mode with live sliders, the hub protocol, music at 10%) leave little to argue about. The 'This computer' section was the most useful part: it names the tools, the stand-ins for hardware that isn't here, and the shared-machine rules, so I could test claims before putting them in the plan instead of guessing. Linking the engine and the hub directly meant the plan could rest on real APIs. I ran about a dozen of its facts here and marked them, such as music defaulting to 10%, the pause menu scaling to TV size, and freeing the D-pad by swapping input presets.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Four things. First, 'Follow the hub library for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own'. The hub's README says that outside a session the game is unaffected, and it defines no network without the hub, so 'on its own' has no defined meaning there. I read it as couch co-op on one machine and said so in the plan, but that is my interpretation. Second, TASK.md is written to the builder, so as the planner I had to work out which parts were mine. STAGE.md settles the title and the file names, but Source Information, the feedback questions and the exit interview were left to inference. I treated them as the builder's job and only made sure the plan leaves room for them. Third, how close 'original game' may sit to 'capture its world, characters, themes and tone', when the title must riff on the source's name. I kept the genre, mechanics and tone and invented every name, character and place. Smaller: it isn't said whether the repository's Emberdeep, a Diablo-style game outside the handoff folder, may be drawn on. I assumed yes because it is MIT and the handoff points to it. Also, STAGE.md says to leave TASK.md's file and folder names out of the plan, while the goal says the plan must cover everything TASK.md asks for. Those two pull against each other on the naming rule. I wrote the name's form with placeholders for everything that differs between builders, none of this run's values, and told each builder that the exact string in its own TASK.md wins.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Sizing the scope. This genre gets its appeal from breadth (classes, loot, co-op, a long campaign), TASK.md forbids stubs, and other agents will build it without being able to ask me anything. I only learned that builders of quite different capability work from these plans by reading a note in the engine's repository (docs/HANDOFF-MATRIX.md). So the plan had to work as a full target and still leave a complete game if a builder runs short. That is why it has a fixed build order and an explicit cut order with a never-cut list. It came out at about 18,000 words, which may be more than some builders can use well, and I can't test that from here. The second hardest was the network design: a horde game has to fit the hub's limit of 20 messages a second, and it needed one design that also covers couch co-op and a host with no player, without each skill needing its own netcode.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: 1) Say in one sentence what multiplayer 'on its own' must be: couch co-op, online without the hub, or just running normally. 2) Tell the planner who the builders are and roughly what budget they have, so the plan can be sized on purpose rather than by a lucky find in the engine's docs. 3) Give a target length for the plan, or say there is no limit. 4) Mark which sections of TASK.md are for the builder only, or give the planner a shorter version without them. 5) Name Emberdeep in the Tech Stack line as allowed reference material for this kind of game: the kit the engine's playbook names for action RPGs is a small adventure game, and Emberdeep is far closer. 6) Say whether the attract mode's 10-second idle rule also applies while Settings or Credits are open. I excluded those screens, but that was a guess. 7) Write STAGE.md's exception into the goal's done-when line, for example 'everything TASK.md asks for, apart from its file and folder names'. As written, the automatic check kept reading 'covers everything' as requiring the literal name that STAGE.md forbids, and the two could not both be satisfied that way.

goalReason: PLAN.md does not contain TASK.md's literal bracketed folder and file name, which TASK.md requires, so 'covers everything TASK.md asks for' is not literally met. The omission follows STAGE.md ('Leave out TASK.md's file and folder names too') and commit e688de41, but the transcript shows no change that reconciles that instruction with the done-when wording. The other requirements are covered, per the section 20 table.
